newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blasts Arafat over land sales comments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blasts Arafat over land sales comments.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday sharply criticised Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, saying it was "dismayed" that he had backed a law imposing the death penalty for land sales to Jews.
"Frankly his comments this morning are comments that we cannot support, are comments that leave us quite puzzled as to why he would say those things," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

Arafat said in an interview published on Wednesday that he backed a recent decision to enforce an old Jordanian law in the West Bank punishing land sales to Jews by death. Jordan ruled the West Bank until Israel occupied the area in 1967.

"The United States condemns any law or any decree that would threaten death against any Palestinian for selling land to Israelis or Jews," Burns said. "That's wrong. It's contrary to what must prevail in the Middle East, which is peace."
"Chairman Arafat must stand up for the rule of law. He must defend it in what he says and what he does," Burns told a news briefing.
"Frankly the recent statements by members of his administration ... inciting Palestinians to attack and murder other Palestinians for selling land, those statements are reprehensible," he added.
Israel said on Wednesday it would complain to the U.N. committee on human rights over the Palestinian Authority's decision.
Burns said U.S. officials including special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, who visited the region last week, had made clear their unhappiness to Palestinian leaders.
The United States at first tried to play down the controversy, casting doubt last week on whether there was any Palestinian decree on the death penalty for land sales.
But Arafat's comments appeared to have left the State Department with no alternative but to react forcefully.
"We are talking about isolated traitors," Arafat said. "And we will impose against them what is on the law books. That is our right and our obligation to protect our land."
Burns said, "We were dismayed to see the public comments by Arafat."
Israel linked the ban on land sales with the recent killings of two Palestinian land dealers found dead in the West Bank. The Palestinian Authority denied any involvement in the killings.
Burns said the United States had no evidence linking the Authority to the murders.

Despite public remarks by a U.S. diplomat in Jerusalem speaking of a high vacancy rate, Burns on Wednesday continued to decline comment on a recent survey in which it reportedly found that many homes in Jewish settlements stand empty.
"I don't believe we're going to make the current analysis, which we've just done, public," he said. "But we are going to share it with the Israelis and with the (U.S.) Congress."

The U.S. consul general in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, said on Tuesday that there was a 25 percent vacancy rate in Jewish settlements in occupied Arab lands, and consequently no need to expand the settlements as Israel wants to do.

Israeli-Palestinian differences over Israel's settlements policy have stalled the Middle East peace process. Arafat on Wednesday called on the United States to put more presure on Israel in order to rescue the process.
